428.title: Bhakti: the Upanishad's last word
428.hook: a sage finishes six chapters of hard teaching and ends on one word: love
428.carry: bhakti: the teaching shines for one who loves
428.tomorrow: what one line holds all the Upanishads?
428.howItsDone: Bhakti is lived across Hindu traditions through kirtan and bhajan singing, temple worship, repeating God's name, and honoring one's teacher, and many devotees treat love of God as the heart of practice.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: anor aniyan, smaller than small, greater than great, hidden in the heart and past the stars. the one in your heart is greater than the sky.

segments.voice: On a festival night at a Hindu temple, the sound can reach the street before you reach the door: bells, drums, a crowd singing one name over and over, someone in tears at the front. That whole world of love poured toward God has a name, bhakti, devotion. You met it in year one with Mirabai and the saints. But where does the word first show up in these old texts? You have to read to the very end of the Shvetashvatara, to its final verse.
screen: `BELLS, DRUMS, ONE NAME SUNG.` → `THE WORLD OF BHAKTI.` → `WHERE DOES THE WORD BEGIN?`

segments.voice: The Shvetashvatara is named for its teacher, and near the end the text tells his story in a few lines. By the power of his tapas, his discipline, and by the grace of God, the wise Shvetashvatara came to know Brahman, and he taught it to seekers who had left everything else behind. Notice the order: his own effort, and then grace. He doesn't take the credit alone. And then the very last verse, 6.23, in paraphrase: for the great soul who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the teacher as to God, these things that have been taught shine out. Highest devotion is para bhakti. Bhakti comes from a root, bhaj, to share, to take part, to belong. Scholars often point to this verse as the first time the word bhakti appears in the principal Upanishads in this sense, devotion to a personal God. Six chapters of wheels, swans and fire sticks, and the last verse doesn't add more knowledge. It says the knowledge shines for the one who loves. That's the teaching Hindus live at every bhajan night and every aarti: God is known by love, not by thinking alone. And the teacher is part of it, which is why a Hindu student bows to the guru, and a young dancer or musician touches the teacher's feet before a lesson. Not everyone reads it alike: Advaita teachers often treat devotion as what readies the mind for knowledge, while devotional schools treat it as the goal itself.

segments.voice: Bhakti is practiced out loud, so try it softly. If you pray, choose one name of God that's yours, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Devi, or simply om, and say or sing it slowly, again and again, for the sit. If you don't pray, say the name of a teacher who gave you something, and let thanks come with it. Let the name do the work, the way one name carries a whole room at a bhajan night.

429.title: Salt in the water: you are that
429.hook: a proud son comes home after twelve years of study, and his father hands him a cup of salt water
429.carry: tat tvam asi: you are that
429.howItsDone: Hindu traditions treat these Upanishads as the heart of the Vedanta: students chant and study them with a teacher, and the great sayings, such as tat tvam asi and prajnanam brahma, are taught as summaries of the whole.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, the Shvetashvatara's last word. The teaching shines for one who loves. Today, the last day of the Upanishads.
screen: `BHAKTI — THE HIGHEST DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Ninety-seven days ago you started with one syllable, om. Seven Upanishads later, the block ends on the story many teachers use to sum up all of them: a father, a son, and a cup of salt water. The son is Shvetaketu. He left home at twelve to study with a teacher and came back at twenty-four, having learned all the Vedas, and, the Chandogya says, very proud of it.
screen: `OM, NINETY-SEVEN DAYS AGO.` → `A FATHER, A SON, A CUP OF WATER.` → `TWELVE YEARS AWAY. VERY PROUD.`

segments.voice: His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question. Did you ask your teachers for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So Uddalaka teaches him, lesson after lesson, through the Chandogya's sixth chapter. One evening he says: put this lump of salt in the water and come back in the morning. In the morning: bring me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. It's gone. Sip from the top, says his father. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. You can't see it, Uddalaka says, but it's here, all through. In the same way, there is a finest essence, and this whole world has it as its self. That is the truth. That is the self. And that, Shvetaketu, you are. Tat tvam asi. Hindus count it among the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and its teaching is the heart of the Upanishads: the self in you, the atman, is not a stranger to Brahman, the reality in everything. And the schools read it differently. Advaita hears one reality without a second. Vishishtadvaita hears a self that belongs to God the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita reads the words another way, keeping the soul and God distinct. All of them treasure it. Many Hindus explain the folded hands of namaste the same way: a bow to the divine in the other person, the coworker who annoys you and the stranger on the bus included. Like the salt, it's in every sip.
screen: `THE UNHEARD BECOMES HEARD?` · `SALTY: TOP, MIDDLE, BOTTOM.` · `THAT, SHVETAKETU, YOU ARE.` · `THREE SCHOOLS, AND NAMASTE.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Sit in the posture from four days ago and take seven breaths, one for each book: salt everywhere; not this, not this; inward, sheath by sheath, to joy; consciousness is Brahman; the breath itself; the river reaching the sea; devotion, in whatever form is yours. Then let the rest of the sit be quiet, with three words underneath it: you are that.

Uddalaka, the sage who taught his son with salt dissolved in water. Ninety-eight sessions in seven of the principal Upanishads, from om at the Chandogya's opening to bhakti in the Shvetashvatara's last verse, carry his thread.

430.title: Patanjali's first word: now
430.hook: a legend says the yoga teacher fell as a tiny serpent into his mother's joined palms; his book opens with one small word
430.carry: yoga is the stilling of the mind
430.tomorrow: when the mind goes quiet, who is left?
430.howItsDone: Students of yoga in many Hindu lineages begin study of the Yoga Sutras with an invocation to Patanjali and by chanting 1.1 and 1.2, often with Vyasa's classic commentary, and treat 1.2 as the definition the whole text unfolds.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Upanishads closed with Uddalaka's three words: tat tvam asi, you are that. Today a new block begins: the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT — BLOCK A, DONE.`

segments.voice: A yoga class at a gym: mats, mirrors, someone holding a long, shaking plank. In some studios there's a small statue up front, and if you look closely, the figure is half man and half serpent, with a hood of snake heads over him. That's Patanjali, the name the Yoga Sutras are gathered under. And Hindus tell a story about how he came.
screen: `MATS, MIRRORS, A SHAKING PLANK.` → `A STATUE, HALF SERPENT.` → `WHO IS PATANJALI?`

segments.voice: A woman named Gonika, the legend goes, a seeker herself, was praying for a son she could pass her learning to. At sunrise she stood in the water and cupped her hands to offer water to the sun, and a tiny serpent dropped into her open palms. Pata, fallen; anjali, joined palms: Patanjali. The serpent, in the story, is Adishesha, the great snake Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. It's a legend, not history, but it says what Hindus believe about this book: it was given, not invented. The book agrees. Sutra 1.1: atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now, marks a beginning: here the real subject starts. A traditional verse says om and atha were the first sounds from the creator's throat, so both are lucky words to begin with. Anushasanam, commentators say, is teaching that comes after: handed down. Then sutra 1.2 gives the definition: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta, the mind. Vritti, a turning, like water in an eddy. Nirodha, stilling. Only three of the sutras even deal with posture. In Hindu tradition, yoga is one of the six classical darshanas, ways of seeing, and its aim is a mind so still that the seer can rest in itself. That's why a class in India may open with om and a bow to Patanjali, and why many students still chant a verse to him before study, honoring him for clearing the mind with yoga, speech with grammar and the body with medicine. The stretch is welcome. The point is the mind.
screen: `PATA: FALLEN. ANJALI: JOINED PALMS.` · `ATHA, NOW. CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA.` · `A DARSHANA: THE POINT IS THE MIND.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Begin the way Patanjali's students do. If you pray, join your palms and say om once, softly; if you don't, just join your palms. Then sit upright and watch the turnings: a thought arrives, swirls, goes. Each time you notice you've been carried off, say one word silently, now, atha, not as a scolding but as a fresh start, and settle back on the breath. Every return is the first sutra, said again.
Now. The first word of the Yoga Sutras, atha: the teaching begins here, and so does the practice, every time you come back.

431.title: King Lavana's dream and the seer
431.hook: a king lives a whole hard lifetime in a magician's spell, then wakes on his throne
431.carry: the seer is not the thoughts it sees
431.tomorrow: how many ways can a mind turn?
431.howItsDone: In Patanjali's yoga, practitioners learn to witness the mind's movements rather than become them, and many Hindu teachers describe meditation as resting as the witness, sakshi, behind thought.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: atha, now, and your line, yoga is the stilling of the mind. So when the turnings go still, what's left?
screen: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Hindus tell a story from the Yoga Vasishtha, a long book of teachings the sage Vasishtha gives to young Rama. King Lavana is sitting in court when a magician walks in and waves a bundle of peacock feathers. The king goes still on his throne. And inside his mind, a whole life begins.
screen: `A KING IN COURT.` → `A WAVE OF PEACOCK FEATHERS.` → `A WHOLE LIFE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: He rides off on a horse into a wilderness and is lost. He marries a woman from a poor forest village, has children, and grows old in hardship. A famine comes, and his children are starving. And then he jolts awake, on his throne, in front of his court, and only a short while has passed. A whole life, and he was sitting there the entire time. Patanjali's next two sutras are about that moment of waking. Sutra 1.3: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then the seer rests in its own form. Then: once the turnings are stilled. Drashtri, the seer: pure awareness, which Patanjali also calls purusha. When the whirling stops, nothing is lost. The seer is left as it always was. Sutra 1.4 covers the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer seems to take the form of the turnings. That's Lavana in the forest. Fear rises, and awareness seems to become fear. A worry spins, and awareness seems to be the worry. The commentators say the seer never really changes; it only looks that way. Here Patanjali leans on an older school, Samkhya, which separates purusha, the seer, from prakriti, everything that changes, the mind included. The mind is the screen. The Vedanta schools, the Yoga Vasishtha among them, describe the seer in their own terms, and many Hindu teachers call it the sakshi, the witness. But on this point they meet: the one who sees is not the passing thoughts it sees. That's what many Hindus who meditate are doing when they sit with closed eyes: not chasing the thoughts, resting as the one who watches them.
screen: `A WHOLE LIFE, ON THE THRONE.` · `THE SEER RESTS IN ITS OWN FORM.` · `OTHERWISE, IT SEEMS TO BE THE TURNINGS.` · `THE SAKSHI, THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE MIND IS THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: Let thoughts come, and notice each one the way you'd notice a scene on a screen: there's a plan, there's a memory, there's a worry. Then lean your attention slightly back toward the one who is noticing, without trying to find or describe it, the way Lavana woke and found himself on the throne he'd never left.

screen: `THE SEER IS NOT THE THOUGHTS IT SEES.`

segments.voice: The Ramayana. In the forest, Sita sees a deer with a coat of gold, flecked like jewels, and she wants it. Rama goes after it. Lakshmana, his brother, warns them: no real deer looks like that. It's the demon Maricha in disguise, sent by Ravana. He's right. Rama's arrow finds the deer, and as it dies, Maricha cries out in Rama's own voice: Ah, Sita! Ah, Lakshmana!
screen: `A DEER WITH A COAT OF GOLD.` → `LAKSHMANA: NO DEER LOOKS LIKE THAT.` → `A CRY IN RAMA'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sita hears the cry and is sure Rama is dying. She sends Lakshmana after him, and with both brothers gone, Ravana comes. One of the great turns of the Ramayana begins with a mind taking something false for real. Read it with Patanjali's list in hand. Sutras 1.5 to 1.11 say every turning of the mind is one of five kinds, and each can bring pain or not. One: pramana, right knowledge, by perception, inference or reliable testimony. Lakshmana had it: no real deer looks like that. Two: viparyaya, error, a picture that doesn't match the real form. A demon seen as a deer. The classic Indian example is a coiled rope at dusk taken for a snake. Three: vikalpa, knowing that follows words with nothing real behind them; Indian logicians liked the example of a hare's horn. Four: nidra, sleep. Patanjali counts even dreamless sleep as a turning; the commentator Vyasa notes that you wake and say, I slept well. Five: smriti, memory, holding on to what you've lived. And here's the twist: right knowledge is on the list. Yoga is the stilling of all five, the true ones too, because even a true thought is the mind moving. Why sort them? Many teachers say a turning you can name loosens its grip. It's a map Hindu meditators have used for centuries: notice the turning, name it, and don't run after it. In the Ramayana, chasing one golden deer cost almost everything. In a sit, naming the turning is how you stop chasing.
screen: `A FALSE CRY. A MIND SURE OF IT.` · `RIGHT KNOWLEDGE AND ERROR.` · `IMAGINING, SLEEP, MEMORY.` · `NAME IT; DON'T CHASE IT.` · then, large: `EVEN TRUE THOUGHTS ARE TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Be a gentle sorter: when a thought arises, give it one of five silent labels. Knowing, a car outside; error, that voice was the fridge; imagining, a conversation that isn't happening; sleep, a drifting fog; memory, something from yesterday. Don't argue with any of them; label, let it pass, and come back to the breath.
Vritti, a turning, a whirl of the mind. Patanjali names five kinds: right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep and memory, the movements yoga learns to still.

433.title: Arjuna's restless mind
433.hook: between two armies, Arjuna tells Krishna the truth: his mind won't hold still
433.carry: abhyasa and vairagya: practice and letting go
433.tomorrow: what did Arjuna see when he aimed at the bird?
433.howItsDone: Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages describe abhyasa and vairagya as the two wings of spiritual life, practiced through daily meditation or prayer kept up over years and a steady loosening of craving.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: vritti, the five turnings, and even true knowing is one turnings of the mind: knowing, error, imagining, sleep and memory. Even true knowing is one.
screen: `FIVE TURNINGS, AND EVEN TRUE KNOWING IS ONE TURNINGS, AND EVEN TRUE KNOWING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavad Gita, chapter six. Two armies wait on the field of Kurukshetra, and in a chariot between them, Krishna has just taught Arjuna how to meditate: sit steady, gather the mind, see the self in all beings. And Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, says what every beginner thinks. Krishna, I don't see how this can last. The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn. Holding it is as hard as holding the wind.
screen: `TWO ARMIES. ONE CHARIOT.` → `THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` → `HOW DO YOU HOLD IT?`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But by abhyasa, practice, and by vairagya, letting go, it can be held. Patanjali gives the same pair in sutra 1.12: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. The turnings are stilled by practice and non-attachment. Practice, 1.13 says, is the effort to stay steady. And 1.14 adds the fine print: it takes root when it's kept up a long time, without breaks, and with devotion, real care. No shortcut is offered. Vairagya, in 1.15, is the mastery of someone who no longer thirsts for things, whether seen or only heard about. Commentators take the second to include rewards promised in scripture, even heaven. So letting go isn't only letting go of dessert. It's letting go of spiritual prizes too. The two balance. Practice without letting go turns grim and grabby; letting go without practice becomes drift. This is how Hindus have kept a spiritual life for centuries: a practice kept for years, not weeks. A grandmother's morning puja. A mala of a hundred and eight beads, turned every day. Prayers at dawn, said whether or not anything seems to happen. That's abhyasa. Doing it without bargaining for results is vairagya, close to what Krishna elsewhere calls acting without clinging to the fruit. Arjuna's honest complaint gets a Hindu answer: not a trick, but two wings.
screen: `YES, THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.` · `ABHYASA: THE EFFORT TO STAY STEADY.` · `LONG, UNBROKEN, WHOLEHEARTED.` · `VAIRAGYA: NO MORE THIRST.` · then, large: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: If you have a mala or any string of beads, use it: one bead for each soft repetition of a name of God, or of om. If you don't pray, count breaths on your fingers instead. That's practice. For the second half, keep going, but let go of wanting the sit to go well, wanting calm, wanting insight. Just return, bead by bead, and want nothing from returning.
Nirodha, stilling. Abhyasa and vairagya, practice and non-attachment, are what still the mind's turnings: the steady effort to return, and the letting go of thirst.

434.title: Arjuna sees only the bird
434.hook: Drona asks his students what they see, and only Arjuna sees nothing but the bird
434.carry: samadhi: the mind gathered on one seed
434.tomorrow: what brings you near, if not talent?
434.howItsDone: Teachers of classical yoga describe samadhi in stages, first with an object of meditation and then beyond any object, and students usually work for years with a single support, such as the breath, a mantra or a divine form.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's restless mind, and Krishna's answer: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go. Today closes a week that crossed from one book into another.
screen: `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA: PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: The Mahabharata. Drona, teacher of the young princes, has a wooden bird set high in a tree, then calls his students one at a time. Aim at the bird, he says, and tell me what you see. Yudhishthira, the eldest, says: the tree, the bird, you, my brothers. Step aside, says Drona. Brother after brother gives the same kind of answer. Then it's Arjuna's turn.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `THE TREE, YOU, MY BROTHERS…`

segments.voice: What do you see? Only the bird. Not the tree, not you. Describe the bird, says Drona. I see only its head. Shoot, says Drona, and Arjuna's arrow takes the head off the bird. Popular retellings make it the bird's eye; either way, everything else has fallen away. Patanjali's school has a word for a mind gathered like that: ekagra, one-pointed, and the commentator Vyasa says that's the kind of mind in which samadhi happens. Samadhi means absorption, the mind so gathered that the scattering stops. Sutra 1.17 describes the first kind, absorption with an object, in four stages from coarse to fine: something physical, then something subtle, then joy, then the bare sense of I am. In every stage the mind still rests on something, a support. Later in the chapter Patanjali calls this samadhi with seed, sabija. Sutra 1.18 describes the other kind: practice lets go of even the support, and only faint traces, the samskaras, remain. No object at all. That's the far end. But nearly every Hindu who meditates starts with a seed: a mantra, a name of God, a lamp's flame, the face of God on the home altar, the breath. It's why so much Hindu prayer is repetition and gazing: the same name a hundred and eight times, the same murti every evening at aarti. One bird. Everything else falls away. So the week ran from bhakti, through tat tvam asi, into a new book: now, the seer, the five turnings, practice and letting go, and today, one seed.
screen: `ONLY THE BIRD. ONLY ITS HEAD.` · `ONE-POINTED: COARSE TO FINE.` · `SABIJA, THEN NO SUPPORT LEFT.` · `A NAME, A FLAME, ONE SEED.` · then, large: `WITH SEED, WITHOUT SEED.`

segments.voice: Give the mind one seed. If you pray, light a diya or a candle before an image of God that's yours, or hold one name; if you don't, use a candle flame or one small object. Rest your eyes and attention on it, the way Arjuna saw only the bird. When the tree and the brothers creep back in, other sounds, plans, thoughts, let them go and come back to the one thing. If even the seed thins out for a moment, let it, without chasing it.
Sabija, with seed. Samadhi that still rests on a support, coarse or subtle, joy or the bare sense of I am, as opposed to absorption with no seed at all.
screen: `SABIJA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: samadhi, the mind gathered on one seed. Only the bird. Week sixty-two, done.
